comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **MuonH · d6144 · 4-of-256 experts · 48 layers — ~707B total / ~22.6B active — 2-rack FSDP, full-feature + host offload**

Scaling the routed pool to **256 experts** (2× the 4-of-128 above) and **sharding the model across 2 racks** (128 GPUs, FSDP over `data`), carrying the full training feature set (**GatedNorm + attention gate + XSA + QB routing**) with **host offloading** of the MuonH optimizer state to pinned host memory.

**Architecture**
- Optimizer: **MuonH** (Newton-Schulz on 2D/3D/4D matrices; distributed NS with QuACK SYRK)
- Routing: **top-4 of 256 experts** (+ 1 always-on shared expert), **QB** (DeepSeek-V3 aux-loss-free) balancing
- Features: **GatedNorm** (post-RMSNorm), **per-head attention gate** (2·sigmoid, zero-init identity), **Exclusive Self Attention (XSA)**
- **48 layers**, **hidden_dim 6144** (48 heads / **12 KV**, head_dim 128), expert intermediate 3072, shared-expert 6144, **512 sliding window**, local:global 5:1, long-rope off
- **Total params: ~707.5B** (routed experts 695.8B) · **Active params: ~22.6B** — unchanged from 4-of-128, since top-k is fixed at 4 and only the pool doubled
- **MoE impl: `sonic_cute` chunk-4** (`SCALE_MOE_EXPERT_CHUNKS=4`, 64 experts/chunk — finer gather/compute overlap; the best config at 2 racks, see below); **host offloading** `SCALE_OFFLOAD_OPT_STATE=1` (opt-state parked on pinned host between steps → HBM freed for the memory-bound scheduler; GB200 NVLink-C2C)
- **Sharding: FSDP over `data=128` across both racks** (`SCALE_REPLICA_AXIS=1`) — 2 experts/GPU, same per-GPU density as the 1-rack 4-of-128

**Throughput (GB200, 2 racks / 128 GPUs, batch 2304, SlimPajama, 12-step probe)**

Cross-rack FSDP is comm-bound; two levers help — larger batch (amortize the InfiniBand weight-gathers; knee ~16–18 seq/GPU) and finer MoE chunking (more gather/compute overlap):

| config | batch | seq/GPU | tok/s | MFU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| chunk-2 | 1,024 | 8 | 265K | 12.0% |
| chunk-2 | 2,048 | 16 | 387K | 17.5% |
| chunk-2 | 2,304 | 18 | 402K | 18.1% |
| **chunk-4** | **2,304** | **18** | **412K** | **18.6%** |

Best = **chunk-4 @ batch 2304: 18.6% MFU / 412K tok/s** (p50 18.63, mean 18.66). Chunk-4 adds **+0.5 pt** over chunk-2 at the same batch — finer chunking hides more of the cross-rack expert-weight gather.

**12-rack / 20T projection**

| | GPUs | batch | tok/s | MFU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **2 racks (measured)** | 128 | 2,304 seq × 4096 (9.4M tok/step) | **412K** | **18.6%** |
| **12 racks (projected)** | 768 | 13,824 seq × 4096 (56.6M tok/step) | **~2.35M** | **~17.7%** |

**Training duration: 20T tokens → ~99 days** at 12 racks (20e12 ÷ 2.35M tok/s). The projection scales the measured 2-rack tok/s by 6× and applies a **~5% weak-scaling penalty for 2→12 racks** — not the 7% used for 1→12 elsewhere: the big cross-rack hit is **already** in the 2-rack number, so 5% (≈ 7% × log₂6 / log₂12) is just the incremental degradation over the smaller 6× span.

The **cross-rack penalty is the dominant cost**: the same full-feature model is ~23% MFU on 1 rack (4-of-128) vs ~18.6% here (4-of-256, 2 racks) — the drop is FSDP weight-gathers + Muon stack reshards crossing the InfiniBand rack boundary instead of NVLink.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **MuonH · d6144 · 4-of-128 · MLA + full-width 72-head attention + learned relative-position bias — ~360B total / ~21.3B active**

d6144 4-of-128 MoE with a Multi-head Latent Attention front-end, **full-width 72-head attention**, **full causal attention on every layer** (no sliding window), and a **learned relative-position bias** replacing RoPE.

**Architecture**
- Attention: **MLA** — `x → c_kv (512)` + learnable RMSNorm → k, v; `x → c_q (2048)` + learnable RMSNorm → q. **Head count 72, head_dim 128 → 9216-wide attention** (wider than hidden 6144, i.e. "full width"). Full MHA: 72 query / 72 KV heads. No QK-norm, no RoPE.
- **Learned relative-position encoding**: factorized per-head bias band — `rel_pos_a` projects x to a per-head latent, `rel_pos_b` (zero-init → NoPE at step 0) maps it to a learned bias over relative offsets. Fused into the FA4 CuTe kernel (forward + `d_bias` backward). This is the positional signal in place of RoPE.
- **Full causal attention on all 48 layers** (sliding window off) — O(S²) over seq 4096.
- Plus XSA, QB (aux-loss-free) routing, GatedNorm, host-offloaded MuonH optimizer state, `sonic_cute` chunk-2 MoE.
- **Total ~360B** · **Active ~21.3B** (4-of-128; attention 4.83B of active from the 72-head/9216 width).

**Throughput (GB200, 1 rack / 64 GPUs, batch 768, SlimPajama, 12-step probe)**

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 rack (measured)** | 64 | 768 seq × 4096 (3.1M tok/step) | **172.5K** | **15.40%** | **~15.6%** |

**Training duration: 20T tokens → ~120 days** at 12 racks (20e12 ÷ 1.93M tok/s). The projection scales the measured 1-rack tok/s by 12× with the standard 7% weak-scaling penalty (1-rack tok/s × 12 × 0.93). **Caveat:** empirically the first cross-rack hop is much costlier than 7% for these FSDP MoE recipes (measured ~19% relative drop 1→2 racks on the full-feature GQA model), so the true 12-rack number likely runs meaningfully below this — treat ~120 days as an optimistic floor.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 **Per-long-layer KV heads: local 16 / global 8 with a static FA4 shape**

The working implementation uses one homogeneous scanned block stack with 16 physical KV heads. Global layers slice the first 8 projected K/V heads and repeat each head twice before FA4; with 48 Q heads, this is numerically equivalent to 8-head GQA because each logical KV head still serves six consecutive Q heads. A same-shaped `where` selects local or global activations, so the differentiated scan contains no shape-changing `lax.cond`.

**Result** — MuonH, d6144, 48 layers, 4-of-128 experts, local:global 5:1, seq 4096, batch 1024, 64 GB200s, 30 steps:

| | GPUs | batch | tok/s | MFU |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 rack measured, median steps 10–28 | 64 | 1,024 × 4096 | **238,547** | **21.553%** |
| 12 racks projected, −7% weak scaling | 768 | 12,288 × 4096 | **~2.66M** | **~20.04%** |

The 12-rack projection gives **~87 days for 20T tokens**. Final loss was 6.0386. All 30 steps, all 16 worker ranks, and the coordinator completed successfully.

This is **4.7% faster** than the working two-stack flat-conditional implementation (227,755 tok/s, 20.578% MFU). Two homogeneous-stack `lax.cond` placements failed before step 0 with CUDA OOM; one requested a contiguous 105.53 GiB allocation per GPU. A uniform-16 control with the same 359,942,670,336 parameters completed, isolating the failure to differentiation through the heterogeneous conditional rather than the padded stack or optimizer. Repeating logical heads into a static physical shape removed that allocation; its post-remat estimate (149.53 GiB) matched the healthy uniform control (149.28 GiB).

**Caveat:** this preserves 8-head GQA semantics on global layers, but it does not recover the parameter, projection, or FA4-kernel savings of physically storing global layers at width 8. The checkpoint stores 16-head K/V weights for every layer; global layers ignore the padded half.

🤖 **MuonH · d5120 · 8-of-256 experts · 48 layers — 249B total / 14.5B active — EP64 fixed all-to-all MoE**

The current-code EP64 run finished 30 steps on one GB200 rack at **17.823% p50 MFU**, **17.814% mean MFU**, and **276.1K tokens/s**. MFU uses the true GB200 bf16 dense denominator of 2.5 PFLOP/s per GPU.

**Architecture**
- Optimizer: **MuonH**, with SYRK enabled
- Routing: **top-8 of 256 routed experts**, plus one always-on shared expert; capacity factor 1.0
- **48 layers**, **hidden_dim 5120** (40 query heads / 10 KV heads, head_dim 128)
- Routed-expert intermediate 1280, shared-expert intermediate 5120, **2048 sliding window**
- **~249B total parameters / ~14.5B active parameters**, excluding embedding and LM-head parameters from the active count
- `gpu_fa4_cute` attention and `ragged_all_to_all` MoE with the fixed-capacity `all_to_all` path
- Expert axis 64: four experts per GPU, confined to one 64-GPU NVLink rack

**Throughput**

| GPUs | Global batch | Tokens/step | Tokens/s | Step time | p50 MFU | Mean MFU | Steps |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 GB200 | 1,024 × 4,096 | 4.19M | **276.1K** | **15.2s** | **17.823%** | **17.814%** | 30 |

Using the issue's 12-rack projection rule (12× batch and 7% lower tokens/s/rack), this is **~3.08M tokens/s** and **~75 days for 20T tokens**. This projection has not been measured at 12 racks.

The pinned reference snapshot reached 17.220% p50 MFU and 266.6K tokens/s. Earlier ragged-path runs varied substantially with node placement, so 17.823% is a measured result for the linked rack run, not yet a placement-insensitive expectation.

**Fixes required on current code**
1. **Keep the batch sharded over the expert axis before EP dispatch.** The canonical batch partition now includes `expert`, avoiding an expertless activation layout at the EP `shard_map` boundary.
2. **Shard non-expert tensors over `data × expert`.** Attention, shared-MLP, LM-head weights, and their optimizer state otherwise replicate when EP64 reduces the `data` axis to one, exhausting device memory before step 1.
3. **Preserve expert sharding through MuonH's stacked 4D Newton–Schulz update.** The layer/expert merge previously materialized the full expert stack on every GPU. Transposing expert ahead of layer keeps the merge local to each expert shard.
4. **Use fixed-capacity `jax.lax.all_to_all` dispatch/combine.** The original ragged collective lowered to many small SendRecv kernels. `SCALE_A2A_CHUNKS=2` bounds activation memory. The nested Fray task now forwards all `SCALE_` variables so this path is actually selected at trace time.
5. **Install the complete CUTLASS DSL 4.6 package.** Removing the obsolete 4.5.2 dependency override restores `cutlass.cute`, which `gpu_fa4_cute` requires.

Flash attention is the large seq4096 lever: reference attention materializes the `[B, heads, S, S]` score tensor. The fixed all-to-all is included in this reproduction, but its measured gain at seq4096 is small because the layer is compute-bound; its larger benefit is expected in shorter-sequence, communication-bound runs. `SCALE_WATCH_INTERVAL=0` and full checkpoint disablement are required for the 30-step run to finish without the step-10 memory spike or final coordinated checkpoint failure.

comments.body:
🤖 **Gather dispatch · MuonH · d5120 · 8-of-256 experts · 48 layers — 249B total / 14.5B active — EP64 fixed all-to-all MoE**

Replacing the fixed-A2A dispatch's repeated-activation scatter with an int32 assignment scatter followed by an activation gather raised one-rack p50 MFU from **17.552% to 20.558%**: **+3.006 MFU points / +17.13% relative**. Both sides ran 120 training steps on 64 GB200s. MFU uses the true GB200 bf16 dense denominator of 2.5 PFLOP/s per GPU.

Relative to the original 17.17% reproduction, the treatment is +3.39 MFU points. That comparison includes `SCALE_A2A_CHUNKS=2 → 1`; the matched A/B below holds chunks at one and isolates gather dispatch.

**Throughput**

| Dispatch construction | p10 MFU | p50 MFU | p90 MFU | Mean MFU | p50 tokens/s | p50 step time | Measured samples |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Repeated bf16 activation scatter | 17.501% | **17.552%** | 17.603% | 17.550% | 271.9K | 15.43s | 119 |
| Int32 assignment scatter + gather | 20.467% | **20.558%** | 20.662% | 20.563% | 318.5K | 13.17s | 119 |

Tokens/s and step time are the p50-equivalent values from the locked FLOPs/example count. The final observed samples were 271.2K and 317.2K tokens/s.

Using the issue's 12-rack projection rule (12× batch and 7% lower tokens/s/rack), the treatment projects to **~3.55M tokens/s** and **~65 days for 20T tokens**. This has not been measured at 12 racks.

<details>
<summary>Architecture, implementation, correctness, profile, and reproduction details</summary>

**Architecture**

- Optimizer: **MuonH**, with SYRK enabled
- Routing: **top-8 of 256 routed experts**, plus one always-on shared expert; capacity factor 1.0
- **48 layers**, **hidden_dim 5120** (40 query heads / 10 KV heads, head_dim 128)
- Routed-expert intermediate 1280, shared-expert intermediate 5120, **2048 sliding window**
- **~249B total parameters / ~14.5B active parameters**, excluding embedding and LM-head parameters from the active count
- `gpu_fa4_cute` attention and `ragged_all_to_all` MoE with the fixed-capacity `jax.lax.all_to_all` path
- Expert axis 64: four experts per GPU, confined to one 64-GPU NVLink rack
- Global batch 1024, sequence length 4096, one fixed-A2A chunk

**Kernel change**

The control repeats each local token eight times, then random-scatters full bf16 rows into the fixed dispatch buffer. At this configuration the repeated activation is about 5.4 GB per GPU. The treatment scatters int32 assignment indices, converts assignment indices to token indices, and gathers rows from `x_local`:

```python
assignment_sources = (
    jnp.full((send_size,), assignments_per_shard, dtype=jnp.int32)
    .at[linear_indices]
    .set(jnp.arange(assignments_per_shard, dtype=jnp.int32), mode="drop")
)
token_sources = jnp.where(
    assignment_sources < assignments_per_shard,
    assignment_sources // topk,
    tokens_per_shard,
)
padded_x = jnp.concatenate(
    [x_local, jnp.zeros((1, hidden_dim), dtype=x_local.dtype)],
    axis=0,
)
send_x = padded_x[token_sources]
```

The fixed-capacity layout, `all_to_all` dispatch/combine, expert MLP, combine weights, and overflow policy are unchanged. The treatment avoids the 8× activation repeat and the full-row random scatter; it does not change the communicated tensor shape.

The treatment is selected with:

```bash
SCALE_A2A_GATHER_DISPATCH=1
SCALE_A2A_CHUNKS=1
```

**Correctness and stability**

- The gather and scatter implementations produced exactly equal forward outputs and dropped-token counts in the kernel test.
- Input, combine-weight, and expert-weight gradients matched at `rtol=atol=1e-5`.
- Both distributed jobs completed 120 finite training steps with descending loss and no OOM, NaN, or Inf.
- The independent distributed loss trajectories were not pointwise bit-exact. Over steps 100–119, scatter averaged 5.81466 and gather averaged 5.87887. The gather-minus-scatter delta averaged +0.06421, with +0.06262 at step 119.

The performance result reproduced. The kernel-level tests support semantic equivalence, but this run did not reproduce the earlier claim that end-to-end loss matches to roughly 0.01 per step.

Both A/B jobs finished the training loop and then failed during the forced final node-local checkpoint after one process disconnected from distributed coordination. Their automatic retries were terminated after the step-119 metrics were preserved. The checkpoint-disabled profile run below finished cleanly.

**Profile**

The treatment profile captured process 0 only, so the XProf session contains one node / four GPUs rather than all 16 nodes. It captured steps 8–10 with HLO proto enabled, host tracer level 1, Python tracer level 0, and XLA command buffers disabled:

```bash
XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer='' --xla_gpu_nccl_termination_timeout_seconds=600"
```

All 16 training tasks and the outer profile job succeeded without retry. The profile run reported 20.401% p50 MFU; use the 120-step A/B for throughput comparison because profiling and disabled command buffers perturb the measurement.

🤖 **MuonH · d6144 · 4-of-128 experts · 48 layers · 2 shared experts — 23.17% → ~24.8% MFU (1 rack) from shared-expert split, Muon shape-grouping, and PGLE**

Stacked increments on the d6144 baseline, all 1 rack (64×GB200), steady-state p50 MFU.

**Architecture**
- Optimizer: **MuonH** (Newton-Schulz), now with **shape-grouped non-expert NS** — same-shape/same-sharding leaves (the 2 shared experts) are concatenated into a single Newton-Schulz call instead of one per leaf.
- Routing: **top-4 of 128 routed experts**, plus **2 always-on shared experts** (the single shared dense expert split into 2 × `hidden_dim/2`; same total shared params).
- **48 layers**, **hidden_dim 6144** (8 KV heads, head_dim 128), routed-expert intermediate 3072, shared-expert intermediate 3072 × 2, 512 sliding window, global every 6.
- **~355B total** (routed experts dominate at 348B) · **~20B active** (top-4/128 + 2 shared, excl. embedding/lm_head).

**Throughput — stacked increments (1 rack, 64×GB200, FSDP intra-rack, muonh, sonic_cute MoE, FA4 CuTe attn)**

| change | p50 MFU | tok/s |
|---|---|---|
| baseline (e128, top-4, 1 shared, batch 1024) | 23.17% | — |
| + 2 shared experts (split into 2 × hidden/2) | 23.46% | 261.9K |
| + Muon shape-grouping (shared-only) | 23.55% | — |
| + batch 1024 → 1152 | 23.70% | 263.0K |
| **+ PGLE (profile-guided latency scheduling)** | **~24.8%** | **276.8K** |

**Projection to 12 racks** (issue rule: 12× batch, −7% tok/s/rack; 20T ÷ 12-rack TPS)

| | GPUs | batch | tok/s | MFU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 rack (measured, best)** | 64 | 1,152 seq × 4096 | **276.8K** | **~24.8%** |
| **12 racks (projected, ×12 × 0.93)** | 768 | 13,824 seq × 4096 (56.6M tok/step) | **~3.09M** | **~23.1%** |

**Training duration: 20T tokens → ~75 days** at 12 racks (vs ~82 days for the prior d6144 4-of-128 point).

**PGLE is the single biggest lever (+1.1 pt), and it is config-only.** Profiling the best run showed the step is exposed-comm-bound on the FSDP expert-weight all-gather (~30% of the step; `bf16[64,6144,6144]` ≈ 4.8 GB/chunk), with the FA4 attention kernel stalling ~1.3 ms per layer waiting on the two MoE-chunk gathers even though its inputs are ready. XLA's latency-hiding scheduler makes the wrong overlap decision from *heuristic* collective latencies; PGLE feeds it *measured* latencies and the overlap recovers. Enabling the latency-hiding scheduler **without** PGLE gives nothing (23.5%) — the win is the measured latencies, not the flag. Reproduced across two runs (24.99%, 24.77%).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Fidelity flag for the EP64 fixed-a2a line (the 17.55% / 20.558% runs above and the follow-ups in #7279): those runs route with QB balancing off — `qb_routing` defaults to False in `launch_cw_scale.py`, and the recorded submit commands never set `SCALE_MOE_QB`. Measured with an exact drop counter at the same operating point, that configuration router-collapses: routed experts drop 85–89% of assignments early in training and oscillate 17–79% over a full 120-step run. The always-on shared expert keeps loss descending, so the collapse is invisible in loss curves.

Two consequences for reading MFU numbers in that regime: dropped-assignment fraction is a fidelity metric those runs do not report, and heavy-drop runs read *higher* MFU (dropped assignments gather a zero pad row and do less real work), so QB-off vs QB-on MFU gaps are upper bounds. With QB on at the same shape: 22.60% p50 at cf1.0 (settles at ~6% drops) and 20.85% at cf1.15 (3.7% at step 119 and declining — the only measured config under the ~3% reference bar).

Full measurements, drop-metric validation, and repro knobs: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7279#issuecomment-5080435482. This flag covers only the EP64 fixed-a2a lineage; QB state for the other tracker rows is being audited separately.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **EP64 with a custom scatter-add adjoint beats the best prior FSDP figure at both architectures we measured, and the fine-granularity result is compliant at 1.44% dropped assignments.**

Both results here are one-rack EP64 with the custom adjoint. The comparison column is the best previously reported FSDP figure for the same architecture, sourced per row below the table.

| architecture | this work (EP64, 1 rack) | drops | prior best (FSDP) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| d6144 · 4-of-128 · 48L | 24.594% | 9–13% | 23.1% |
| d6144 · 4-of-128, compliant (projected) | ~23.9% | ≤3% | 23.1% |
| d5120 · 8-of-256 · i1280 · 48L | **20.708%** | **1.44%** | 19.2% |
| d5120 · 8-of-256, at a 5% bar | 21.849% | 3.66% | 19.2% |

Sources for the comparison column: **23.1%** is the full-feature + host-offload d6144 4-of-128 result in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5036748495 (255.3K tok/s, one rack measured); **19.2%** is the "fine granularity" row of the "Measured architecture data points (GB200)" table in this issue's body (two-rack measurement). Details and caveats below.

## d5120 · 8-of-256 · i1280 — measured compliant

350-step legs on one allocation draw, drop fractions are true 100-step tails, QB-on, custom adjoint:

| spill m | capacity factor | p50 MFU | tail-100 drops |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 1.0 | 22.062% | 7.10% |
| 3 | 1.0 | 21.849% | 3.66% |
| 3 | 1.05 | 20.670% | 1.72% |
| **3** | **1.0625** | **20.708%** | **1.44%** |
| 0 | 1.15 | 20.416% | 2.60% |

Against the 19.2% figure: **+1.5pp while dropping under 1.5% of routed assignments**, or **+2.6pp at 3.66%** under a 5% bar.

The mechanism buying the fidelity is same-step spill — when a token's chosen expert bucket is full, the assignment is re-offered to the next-ranked expert *that token already selected* if that bucket has headroom, rather than dropped. Bucket layout, capacity and the fixed-capacity all-to-all are unchanged. It costs 0.213pp and halves drops, cheap for a structural reason: expert GEMMs run on capacity-sized buffers whether or not a slot is filled, so spill adds index work, never matmul work. Combining it with a small capacity increase beats buying capacity alone on both axes — 20.708% at 1.44% versus 20.416% at 2.60%.

## d6144 · 4-of-128 — the one-rack hero candidate

`/mwittmann/ep25d5-d6144-e128-bf16-120-0726-1140-v3`, 120/120 steps, 16/16 tasks: EP64 · batch 1024 · seq 4096 · QB-on · capacity factor 1.0 · host offload · default BFC allocator at the default 0.75 fraction · sliding window 2048. Steady tail (steps 90–119) p10 24.434 / p50 24.594 / p90 24.771, sd 0.118, 276.4K tok/s, 15.174 s/step, loss 10.31 → 5.59.

**Plan against ~23.9%, not 24.594%.** The raw figure is measured at 9–13% dropped assignments; applying the measured cost of capacity factor 1.05 plus spill (about −0.65pp) to reach a ≤3% bar still exceeds 23.1%. A run that drops more reads higher MFU, because dropped assignments gather a zero pad row and do less real work, so the raw number should not be compared to a low-drop configuration without that adjustment.

## Caveats

- **The drop fractions of both prior figures are unmeasured**, so both comparisons are one-sided on fidelity. Those runs compute a per-layer drop count but never emit it; the tracker-logging fix is one line and would settle it permanently for one job's cost. This is the largest uncertainty on both results.
- The 19.2% figure is a two-rack measurement while the 8-of-256 result here is one rack, so that comparison bundles parallelization, the adjoint and spill together rather than isolating a parallelization delta. The 23.1% d6144 figure is one rack, so that comparison is rack-matched.
- The 4-of-128 run uses sliding window 2048 where the 23.1% configuration uses 512 with 5:1 local:global, so it does **more** attention work; it also lacks XSA, the attention gate, and GatedNorm, which that configuration has. Both point the same way.
- The 8-of-256 drop figures are 350-step tails and the 4-of-128 figure is 120-step; they are not comparable to each other. The LR schedule is defined over `num_train_steps`, so a given step index sits at a different schedule position in runs of different lengths, and drops fall as the learning rate anneals.
- Capacity factor below 1.0 cannot help: total capacity is exactly `cf × total_assignments`, so drops are bounded below by `1 − cf` regardless of routing.

## Two inputs for choosing between candidates

**4-of-256 at EP64 does not fit one rack**, measured on all 16 tasks: 92.02 GiB resident plus a single 106.63 GiB temp arena against 184.3 GiB physical, so no memory fraction closes it. The resident set decomposes exactly into expert parameters, MuonH momentum and the replicated embedding trio — nothing is mis-sharded. Consistent with the 4-of-256 candidate command above, which already assumes two racks plus offload.

**Drop recovery is bounded by routing granularity.** Spill can only re-offer an assignment to an expert the token itself selected, so top-4 shapes have at most 3 attempts and saturate there — measured through the shipping kernel, the drop fraction is flat from m=3 through m=7 at 4-of-256, while 8-of-256 keeps improving from 2.73% to 1.57%. Top-4 also carries a higher statistical floor, since the per-bucket mean load halves. Neither top-4 candidate reaches a 3% bar by spill alone at capacity factor 1.0; they need capacity headroom on top, at roughly −0.58pp per +0.05.

Method, the full frontier including a falsified capacity-alignment hypothesis, and the reproduction knobs are in #7279.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Receiver-ECHO · MuonH · d5120 · 4-of-256 experts · 48 layers — 394.8B total / ~13.0B active — one-rack EP64 BF16**

The 20-step EP64 screen completed on 16×4 GB200 GPUs with **24.153% median MFU**, **462,267 tokens/s**, and **9.073 s/step** over steps 5–19. The MFU uses the true GB200 BF16 dense denominator of 2.5 PFLOP/s per GPU. Mean exact aggregate post-ECHO assignment drop over the same window was **2.765%**; final loss was finite at **7.945**.

All 16 Iris tasks and 64 ranks completed 20/20 steps with zero failures, preemptions, or retries. This is a short performance screen, not a long-run stability or drop-rate qualification.

| Run | Median MFU | Median step | Median throughput | Mean assignment drop | Final loss |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Matched control | 22.374% | 9.795 s | 428,217 tok/s | 2.918% | 7.943 |
| Padded, stack-sharded non-expert Muon | 24.153% | 9.073 s | 462,267 tok/s | 2.765% | 7.945 |

<details>
<summary>Architecture, kernel path, semantics, validation, and reproduction</summary>

### Architecture

- 48 layers, hidden size 5,120
- 256 routed experts, top-4 routing
- routed expert intermediate size 2,048
- one shared expert with intermediate size 5,120
- global batch 1,024, sequence length 4,096, sliding window 512
- MuonH with SYRK; BF16 training
- EP64 on 16 nodes × 4 GB200 GPUs, one process per GPU
- 394,844,428,288 total parameters; approximately 13.0B active non-embedding parameters per token

### Kernel path

- FA4 CuTe attention
- fixed-shape BF16 token all-to-all
- receiver-pooled ECHO with same-expert clones, sparse clone weights, two padding experts, and at most ten receiver expert segments
- two sender-balanced pipeline chunks
- Sonic dispatch, slot gather, and combine
- SM100 grouped expert GEMMs and grouped weight gradients
- quantile balancing enabled
- XLA latency-hiding scheduler with collective-overlap limit 4
- CUDA command buffers enabled; PGLE disabled for the matched screen

### Receiver-ECHO and drop semantics

An accepted routed assignment executes the router-selected expert, either on its home shard or on a same-expert receiver clone. The path is not dropless: fixed receiver envelopes remain bounded, and assignments that exceed those envelopes are dropped. The reported 2.765% is the exact aggregate assignment drop after ECHO placement, averaged over steps 5–19; it is not a whole-token drop rate.

### Muon change

Five 48-layer non-expert Muon parameter stacks are zero-padded to 64 rows so the Newton–Schulz batch can shard across the 64-way expert mesh. The padded result is resharded directly to the original parameter layout before slicing, so the padded stack is not replicated on every device. Dummy rows remain zero and are removed before applying the update.

The implementation is in [`497423bc6`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/497423bc6716ad102fc53ebdebd7bfdb38304dcc). Local BF16 checks covered square and both rectangular matrix orientations and produced identical padded/unpadded updates. Repository tests also assert that the padded result returns with the original shape and sharding.

### Validation scope

- The matched rack A/B changed only `SCALE_MUON_PAD_NONEXPERT=0` to `1`.
- Both runs used `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=false` and completed without Iris retries.
- The rack losses ended at 7.943 and 7.945 after 20 steps.
- No XProf/HLO capture was taken after enabling padded Muon; the available profile predates this optimizer change.

### Reproduction

From snapshot [`1a88e1f3b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/1a88e1f3be7c26673664922e409234226952a068), with `WANDB_API_KEY` set externally:

```bash
JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=false SCALE_MUON_PAD_NONEXPERT=1 \
  .agents/projects/7201-ep64-drop3/run_best_bf16_ep64.sh \
  ep30-cx-muon-pad-nopgle-20260727-0714 32536 20
```

The submission script is [permalinked here](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a88e1f3be7c26673664922e409234226952a068/.agents/projects/7201-ep64-drop3/run_best_bf16_ep64.sh). The research branch is [`research/rav/7201-ep64-muon-pad`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/rav/7201-ep64-muon-pad).

### Run artifacts

- Padded Muon: [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/rav_moe/runs/ep30-cx-muon-pad-nopgle-20260727-0714) · [Iris](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fep30-cx-muon-pad-nopgle-20260727-0714)
- Matched control: [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/rav_moe/runs/ep30-cx-muon-control-nopgle-20260727-0714) · [Iris](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fep30-cx-muon-control-nopgle-20260727-0714)
- Append-only investigation log: [`7201-ep64-mfu.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a88e1f3be7c26673664922e409234226952a068/.agents/logbooks/7201-ep64-mfu.md)

</details>

🤖 **Long-context sweep — final d6144 stack, seqlen 4k → 8k → 65k at constant ~4.19M tokens/step (1 rack)**

Same [final 1-rack option](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5093392733) (d6144, 48L, hetero-KV 12/6, MTP-1× dense, MoE-chunks 2, sliding-window 512, global-every-6). Each run holds **tokens/step fixed at ~4.19M** by halving batch as seqlen grows, so this isolates the pure cost of longer sequences.

| seq | batch | seq/GPU | tok/s | vs 4k | reported MFU | **true MFU** | wandb |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4k | 1024 | 16 | 246 K | — | 22.24% | **20.6%** | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/d6144-het126-mlp1x-cond-ch2-v1) |
| 8k | 512 | 8 | 241.6 K | **−1.8%** | 23.75% | **20.3%** | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d6144-64gpu-seq8k-b512-ch2-v1) |
| 65k | 64 | 1 | 160.7 K | **−35%** | 36.45% | **17.0%** | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d6144-64gpu-seq65k-b64-ch2-v1) |

**Findings**
- **8k context is nearly free**: −1.8% tok/s, true efficiency flat (~20.4%). Sliding-window 512 means the 40 local layers don't grow — only the 8 global layers pay more.
- **65k costs −35% tok/s** and true efficiency drops to **17%** (the 8 global layers do genuine 65k² attention + 1-seq/GPU parallelism hurts utilization). It **fits** — FA4 + sliding-window keeps 65k in HBM, no OOM.
- **The reported MFU is misleading and gets worse with seqlen.** `lm_flops_per_token` is window-blind: it counts full O(seq²) attention on *all* 48 layers, but 40 are windowed to 512. That overcounts FLOPs by **×1.08 at 4k, ×1.17 at 8k, ×2.14 at 65k** — so reported MFU *rises* (22→24→36) while true efficiency actually *falls* (20.6→20.3→17.0). Trust tok/s; treat MFU as inflated whenever seqlen ≠ 4k. Fix is a window-aware attention term (`min(seq, window)` on local layers, full on global).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Main thoughts on above comment-
going from 48 heads to 64 heads only drops tps from 262k to 243k, a 7% drop. This is a bit of a sweep spot in that this doesn't increase our parameter count by much due to kv cache (1-2B params total sharded over 64 gpus), doesn't increase MFU much due to efficiency of FA4, and doesn't increase saved activation memory at all. Will test quality later, but I expect it to help quality by more than 7%. This is also the same ratio used by Inkling. We can't expand MoE in the same way without hitting OOM pressure. If it were possible to fit more total expert parameters on a single rack that would be great. It is definitely possible in theory but I haven't found it. Increasing active experts while not increasing total experts will likely have limited gains. Our sparsity rate is also not that high, so would rather go sparser than less sparse.

Sliding window impact seems noisy. Sometimes 2048 runs faster than 1024. Will do more quality tests here. conv will likely get included.

Other thing to note here is that 256e / top-8 / routed-1536 (= same total params) is viable, for a 7% tps hit. Potentially worth it, will be close. Didn't test changing MoE chunk count here.

Our watch step is killing mean MFU, it runs at like 2 MFU. This job has watch every 20. Ideally we could make that step faster. I don't understand why its so slow. If not, watch every 40 might be worth it. Though it may cause us to miss some gradient spikes.

comments.body:
This issue has gone un-updated a while so wanted to add in a summary

August 2 — EP64 becomes competitive. On the then-current d5120 hero, the optimization ladder went from ragged EP64 at 260k tok/s / 15.0% median MFU, through fixed-capacity dispatch at 315k / 19.4%, gather dispatch at 360k / 21.9%, and structured custom VJPs at 389k / 24.1%. The selected stack sustained 383k tok/s / 23.7% median MFU over 200 steps. [Final 200-step result](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7279#issuecomment-5155747793)

August 5 — matched EP beats FSDP. On the same d6144, 4-of-128 shape and one rack, EP64 reached 316k tok/s / 27.8% median MFU, versus FSDP’s 235k / 19.4%. EP was doing less work because it dropped about 10% of assignments; correcting for that still left it around 25.5% MFU, roughly six points ahead. [Matched comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7279#issuecomment-5167162893)

August 7–8 — FSDP optimization sweep adds about 9%. Small-parameter sharding plus pre-gather gate/up interleaving took the one-rack FSDP hero from 19.37% to 21.30% MFU, a replicated 7.9–9.1% throughput gain. The best measured step was 16.43 seconds, about 255k tok/s. Much of the gain later shrank after the one-process-per-GPU merge increased peak memory, so this is an optimization milestone rather than the current production number. [Sweep conclusion](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8054#issuecomment-5223621862)

August 8 — first strong d6144 LatentMoE candidate. The d6144, 4-of-192, i6272 EP64 candidate measured 262,396 tok/s on one rack, with 546B total and roughly 25B active parameters. This became the main EP/FSDP decision candidate. [Candidate comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8062#issuecomment-5227823324)

August 14 — current 8-of-384 hero establishes its accepted baseline. The selected three-stripe fixed EP layout sustained 256,818 tok/s / 24.03% median MFU over steps 150–199 of a 200-step run, with 2.41% median drops. This is the most relevant current-shape reference; earlier raw tok/s records are not directly comparable. [Selected 8-of-384 result](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7279#issuecomment-5294194777)

August 16 — stock ragged EP gains 1.62 MFU points on the current hero. QuACK tile, persistence, and per-call-site cluster tuning moved the full 8-of-384 EP64 shape from 223k tok/s / 20.20% MFU to 241,116 tok/s / 21.82% MFU, with zero drops and unchanged loss. Follow-up work established that this path tops out near 22% because transport competes with expert GEMMs for SMs. [Tuning result](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5308322722), [final ceiling](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5313789958)

August 16–17 — fused Marin EP reaches 247k tok/s. On the older 4-of-192 shape, fused transport plus Pallas Blackwell ragged-dot expert GEMMs improved the step from about 18.1 to 17.0 seconds, or roughly 247k tok/s / 22.6% MFU, at 0.5–0.6% drops. Strategically important, but not directly comparable to the selected 8-of-384 hero. [Marin EP tracker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8311)

August 17 — current hero reaches 25.3% MFU at node scale. The 8-of-384 shape ran on four GB200s at 47.4–48.4k tok/s / 25.08–25.56% MFU, with zero drops after step 19. This validates the compute path and shows top-8 itself does not reduce MFU, but it is not an EP64/rack throughput result; the rack-scale transport remains blocked. [Node-scale result](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8108#issuecomment-5312955273)

spillover_issues.title: GB200 Architecture TPS Tracker

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

The Data Belay judge merged in #11019 gives signal on the 176 Datakit sources. Every test fixed in advance passes, except two inconclusive results: T7 for the knowledge group at d768, and T3's verdict agreement at d1024 (79% against an 80% bar). Null arms and dilution references read `no gain` at every rung. 12 of 12 retests on new seeds give the same verdict. Gain Δ correlates at r = 0.84 to 0.99 between two model families and between rungs. Math sources gain on math, code on code, English web on commonsense, and none of the 16 multilingual, 10 legal or 9 safety sources reads yes. Four weaknesses remain: at d1024, calls near the 1% floor depend on which 3 seeds ran; the knowledge group and CruxEval-O sit near noise; the harm check is underpowered at 3 seeds; and the run-on rule sends sources to d1024 that cannot end as a yes. The sweep is done (2026-11-17 09:30 UTC): 49 of 176 sources end yes, 21 mixed and 106 no. The final d1024 numbers and the list of yes sources are in [this comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11582#issuecomment-6944197467).

## Description

Data Belay judges a candidate dataset by training at a 20% share of the base mix and comparing answer loss on 6 eval groups (Paloma, Uncheatable, knowledge, commonsense, math, code) against two baselines. The gain is measured against a control that trains on the base mix alone. The harm is measured against 4 dilution references, which put the same 20% share into text that no eval measures (Japanese ClimbLab, Chinese, Thai and Arabic FinePDFs). Gain Δ is the relative change in a group's loss against the control, so negative is better. A group is `better` when its interval is below 0 and Δ is at least 1% in size (the 1% floor). It is `worse` when its harm interval is above the group's harm limit, which is the larger of 1% and 2.5 control seed SDs, computed from the d512 controls and used at every rung. Verdicts per rung are `helps`, `trade-off` (a better group and a group whose harm is unresolved), `no gain` and `hurts`. A yes is `helps` or `trade-off`.

Each source climbs a ladder of rungs (d512, d768, d1024) and stops after no at two consecutive rungs. One exception, the run-on rule: after two no's, a source still climbs if some group's Δ at the second rung is below 0. At the top rung, a source ends `yes` when d768 and d1024 both say yes, and `mixed` when they disagree. The judge is `experiments/data_belay/judge.py`.

Two models: "main's model" is the dense fast-track model on the main branch (`h100_ladder_model`), and "vanilla" is the vanilla Grug model, which ran the same sweep earlier.

Setup: main's model, one 8×H100 node per run on cw-us-east-02a at batch priority, 3 seeds per arm.

| Rung | Active params | Tokens | Median training time |
|---|---|---|---|
| d512 | 18M | 362M | 4.0 min |
| d768 | 53M | 1.07B | 12.3 min |
| d1024 | 145M | 2.89B | 45.5 min |

The candidates are the 176 Datakit caches at 20% that are not references. Three small sources prepared at 5 to 15% are left out because no references exist at those shares (#11481). Vanilla gives a second model family for replication (T3).

## Hypothesis or Goal

The tests and their pass and fail thresholds were written before the first run (2026-11-14 12:05 UTC):

- T1 Null calibration: extra control seeds judged as a candidate against control seeds 0-2 read `no gain`.
- T2 References: each reference judged against the other three reads `no gain`.
- T3 Cross-model replication: per group, gain Δ on main's model and vanilla correlate at r ≥ 0.8, and yes/no verdicts agree for ≥ 80% of sources. Fails at r < 0.5 or agreement < 70%.
- T4 Test-retest: 12 sources on seeds 3 to 5 agree on yes/no for ≥ 10 of 12. Fails below 8.
- T5 Rung consistency: per group, d512 and d768 gain Δ correlate at r ≥ 0.7. Fails below 0.4.
- T6 Face validity: math sources better on math, code sources on code, non-English sources `no gain` like the references.
- T7 Signal over noise: a group's SD of Δ across sources is ≥ 3× the Δ noise between two 3-seed arms of the same data. Fails below 1.5×; in between is inconclusive.

## Status

d512: 176 sources judged. d768: 176 judged (20 `helps`, 42 `trade-off`, 114 `no gain`). No source reads `hurts`. d1024: 87 judged (23 `helps`, 21 `trade-off`, 43 `no gain`; 85 also on vanilla). 19 are counted as two-rung ladders: their cache is too small for d1024's 2.89B tokens without repeating it more than 4 epochs, which `train` refuses. The other 70 stopped at d768. Final answers: 49 yes, 21 mixed, 106 no. The tables below were computed with 78 d1024 sources; the comment linked in the TL;DR has the final d1024 numbers, which change T3's d1024 agreement to 79%.

| Test | Result | Pass? |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | 4 null arms (control seeds 6-8, 9-11 and 12-14 at d512; 3-5 at d768): all `no gain` | yes |
| T2 | 4 of 4 references `no gain` at d512, d768 and d1024 | yes |
| T3 | Pearson r per group: d512 0.84-0.97 (175 sources), d768 0.87-0.98 (176), d1024 0.92-0.99 (85). Yes/no agreement: 89%, 97%, 79% | yes at d512 and d768; inconclusive at d1024 |
| T4 | 12 of 12 retests give the same verdict | yes |
| T5 | d512 vs d768 r = 0.89 (knowledge) to 0.99 (math). d768 vs d1024 r = 0.90 to 0.99 | yes |
| T6 | Yes at d768, with the median Δ over the category's sources: math 9 of 10 (math −7.7%), code 10 of 18 (code −3.3%), English web 13 of 16 (commonsense −2.3%), agent traces 15 of 46 (12 better on code). Multilingual 0 of 16, legal 0 of 10, safety 0 of 9, bio 0 of 5 | yes |
| T7 | Spread over noise on main's model, d512 / d768: Paloma 8.4× / 7.8×, Uncheatable 5.8× / 5.9×, knowledge 4.7× / 2.1×, commonsense 4.3× / 4.2×, math 9.6× / 6.7×, code 6.5× / 3.4× | yes, except knowledge at d768 (inconclusive) |

Sources that do not match an eval group read `no gain` with groups 0.5 to 4% worse than the control. That cost is the 20% share they take from the base mix, and the dilution references show the same cost, so the judge does not count it as harm.

### Where the method is weak

1. At d1024 the two models' yes/no verdicts differ for 15 of 76 sources, almost all near the 1% floor. 24 groups are `better` only on vanilla and 4 only on main's model. The effects are similar: in those 24 groups, the median Δ is −1.76% on vanilla and −1.18% on main's model. The intervals differ more: their median half-width is 1.29% on vanilla and 2.15% on main's model. Each model's flips fall in the groups where its own 3 d1024 control seeds varied more. Main's model's control varies more on knowledge (CV 0.99% vs 0.52%), commonsense (0.60% vs 0.32%) and code (0.34% vs 0.15%). Vanilla's varies more on math (1.21% vs 0.58%), and 3 of the 4 groups better only on main's model are math. With 3 seeds, a gain of 1 to 2% at d1024 is decided by noise in the estimated spread.
2. Knowledge and CruxEval-O sit near noise. Knowledge is 2.1× at d768. Per task on vanilla d512, CruxEval-O is 1.4×, TriviaQA 1.6× and the MMLU-Pro choice loss 2.2×, against HumanEval+ 6.8× and GSM8K 6.1×. Two code sources that read `helps` on vanilla and `no gain` on main's model improve HumanEval+ and MBPP+ on both models; CruxEval-O pulls the code group's mean toward 0 on main's model.
3. The harm check is underpowered. The median harm-interval half-width is about equal to the harm limit (vanilla d512: Paloma 0.87% against a 1.00% limit). 63 of 71 unresolved groups behind d512 trade-offs had a harm Δ under half the limit. The cause is the number of values: Welch's test on 3 seeds against 4 reference means has 3 to 5 degrees of freedom. The spread between references is not the cause, because the SD between reference means is close to the seed SD / √3.
4. The run-on rule spends d1024 runs that cannot produce a final yes. It sent 26 of the 78 sources judged at d1024, all no at d512 and d768. 3 of the 26 read yes at d1024, and each ends `mixed`, because a final yes also needs a yes at d768. The 26 sources cost 78 training runs (3 seeds each) of about 45 min on 8 H100s.

### Data checks

- hplt_v3 and Nemotron CC v2.1 `*_translated` are English text (100% ASCII in sampled rows). Their `helps` fits the English web category.
- Format learning: eval-format markers ("the answer is", multiple-choice options) in 600 sampled rows per source correlate with math gains (Spearman −0.45 with GSM8K), but they track math content. Sources in eval format without math content gain little (nemotron_specialized_v1_1-multiple_choice moves no task by more than 3%). We found no evidence that format alone drives a verdict.
- Contamination: the decontamination flag rate correlates with gain Δ (Spearman −0.27 to −0.57), but it is confounded with domain. A real scan is #11480.
- The base mix is Datakit text. We have not checked whether it already contains each candidate.

### Proposed judge changes

1. Drop CruxEval-O from the code group, or down-weight it.
2. Train 4 more dilution references, to give the harm test 8 reference values (#11481).
3. Narrow the run-on rule so that it only sends sources whose d768 verdict could still pair with a yes, or remove it.
4. Use more than 3 control seeds at d1024, or pool the control's seed variance across rungs, so one rung's 3-seed spread does not decide calls near the floor.

## Links

* PR: #11019 (merged into main, judge at `cc81637340`)
* W&B: runs `dbelay-main-<rung>-<source>-s<seed>` in [marin-community/marin_moe](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe); vanilla runs are `dbelay-<rung>-...`
* Choice scores: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/data_belay/choice/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fdata_belay%2Fchoice%2F))
* Follow-ups: #11478, #11479, #11480, #11481

## Decision Log

- 2026-11-14: tests T1 to T7 fixed before the first run.
- 2026-11-14: harm limits computed from the d512 controls (max of 1% and 2.5 control seed SDs). `report` refuses a share that has no references.
- 2026-11-14: CC BY, CC BY-SA and ODC-By licenses allowed.

## Conclusion

The judge separates sources by content, repeats across seeds, rungs and model families, and reads `no gain` on null and reference arms. Calls near the 1% floor are not stable at 3 seeds, especially at d1024 and in the knowledge group. d1024 results are in the comment linked in the TL;DR.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

The current evidence answers the title's question yes for source ranking: null and dilution-reference arms read `no gain`, all 12 seed retests agree, and cross-model gain correlations range from 0.84 to 0.99. T7 is inconclusive for knowledge at d768, and d1024 calls near the 1% floor depend on three control seeds. The remaining work is a sweep completion and judge calibration, so a single `Fixes #11582` PR would close this record early.

Plan:
1. Finish the eight running d1024 arms and the `nsf_awards` d512 retry; score all finished seeds. Publish a source-level table for all 176 candidates with rung verdicts, final ladder outcomes, run IDs, and explicit reasons for the 19 two-rung and 71 stopped ladders. Update the issue's TL;DR, T1–T7 results, and conclusion.
2. Preserve the current verdicts, then add d1024 control seeds and retest candidates near the 1% floor. Compare intervals and verdict flips on the same candidates before choosing a control-variance estimate.
3. Make separate, reviewable judge changes: remove the run-on after two consecutive no verdicts in [`ladder_step`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/data_belay/judge.py#L215-L226), since it cannot yield a final yes; ablate CruxEval-O before changing the code group; and test four additional independent dilution references before changing harm calls. [#11481](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11481) tracks references at other shares, not the reference count at 20%.
4. Replay T1–T7 and publish old/new group calls and ladder outcomes before adopting a revised judge. Keep the scorer, contamination scan, and share catalog work in [#11478](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11478), [#11480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11480), and #11481.

spillover_issues.title: [data_belay] Datakit sweep on main's model: does the judge give signal?

spillover_issues.author: davidlundgren
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

A review of 7,503 sampled documents from the 10.05 SFT training mix found a clean chat template and four recurring classes of data flaw: long reasoning that ends in a guess presented as an answer, low-value and contaminating documents in the long-context replay, artifacts left by data conversion, and agent traces that claim success without evidence. Most are detectable by script. The first three recommended filters touch sources that make up more than half of the mix.

## Description

The 10.05 SFT run (`grug-67b-sft-20260929-special-token-lr-full-ab-4750-grouped`, exported as `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05`) trained on 216 SFT token stores (79.65% of training positions) and 391 pretraining replay caches (20.35%). About 80% of the mix is text generated by other open-weight models.

Method:

- **Sample:** 7,503 whole documents drawn at random from the token caches, with per-source count `max(4, round(share × 6000))`, seed 1. Counts in the sample track training share.
- **Clipping:** documents over 16,000 tokens were reviewed as their first 12,000 and last 4,000 tokens. This applies to 3,760 documents, including every long replay document and 643 of 650 open SWE traces.
- **Reviewers:** ten LLM agents. Nine each took one slice. One ran a scripted template audit over all 5,280 SFT documents. Each measured prevalence by script over its whole slice and then read documents closely.
- **Citations:** examples are `source #doc_index`, the document's index in the source cache. "Share of mix" is the combined share of the sources where a flaw occurs, which is an upper bound on what the flaw touches.

| Slice | Documents | Share of mix |
|---|---:|---:|
| Nemotron math | 1,925 | 32.07% |
| Replay, over 64k tokens | 1,398 | 18.09% |
| Nemotron code | 784 | 12.99% |
| Open SWE traces | 650 | 10.83% |
| Nemotron chat and agentic | 649 | 10.33% |
| Nemotron multilingual | 540 | 8.84% |
| AgentTrove, GLM and small sets | 212 | 3.23% |
| Replay, 64k tokens or fewer | 825 | 2.26% |
| Penfever traces | 520 | 1.36% |

## Hypothesis or Goal

Find flaws in the 10.05 mix that could teach the model a bad habit, estimate how common each is, and propose filters or transforms for the next SFT data build.

## Findings

Severity is the reviewer's judgment of harm × prevalence × share of mix.

### 1. Reasoning gives up and the answer hides it (high, 28.4% of mix)

Long reasoning ends in a guess or placeholder, and the final answer states it without a caveat. Prevalence rises with length.

| Source | Prevalence | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `nemotron_sft_v3/math_v3/train` | 43 of 973 documents (8.9% of its tokens); 9 of 56 over 40k tokens, 0 of 224 under 4k. 11 of 12 hits opened were real. | `#1871519` (106k tokens), reasoning: "I'll ignore the covering issue and present this as the answer. Many might accept it… I'm not sure." The answer then asserts the construction "satisfies both conditions". |
| `nemotron_sft_v3/competitive_programming_v2/competitive_coding_python` | 16 of 280; all over 50k tokens (16 of 91 that long). 7 ship the code with no caveat. | `#508`, answer: `# This is a placeholder – it does NOT compute the correct answers.` `#11027`, reasoning: "I'll provide a naive solution… The user may not mind." |
| `…/competitive_coding_cpp` | 5 of 278 | `#270153`: "placeholder that reads the input and outputs a dummy answer" |
| `nemotron_sft_v3/science_v2/vendor` | 79 of 176 have a give-up or guess phrase in the last 3,000 characters of reasoning; 31 exceed 64k tokens | `#29316` (116k tokens): "Final answer guess… I'm not confident… Given the lack of time, I'll output a reasonable IUPAC name." |

### 2. Long-context replay is about half data dumps and machine output (high, 18.1% of mix)

Shares for replay documents over 64k tokens, weighted by true token count (heuristic, about ±3 points):

| Content | Documents | Tokens |
|---|---:|---:|
| Natural documents (reports, theses, books, manuals) | 48.9% | 29.1% |
| Structured data (JSON, CSV, XML, logs, SQL, numeric tables) | 26.5% | 41.8% |
| Machine junk (minified JS, source maps, base64, raw binary, lock files) | 4.5% | 9.0% |
| HTML | 4.5% | 5.7% |
| Human-written code | 5.2% | 5.2% |
| Whole-document tables | 3.9% | 4.1% |
| Library OCR scans | 2.4% | 3.5% |
| SWE-style synthetic documents | 4.2% | 1.6% |

- By a strict definition, 433 of 1,398 documents and 50.8% of tokens are low-value.
- 273 documents (19.5%) exceed the 262,144-token training context and hold 62.4% of the slice's tokens. 63 exceed 1M tokens.
- Quality tiers do not separate junk: the low-value token share is 57% in `q0`, 60% in `q1`, 49% in `q2`, 41% in `q3`, 42% in `q4`.
- Examples: `replay/c01/q0/gt_64k #99358` is a 5.3M-token Python pickle (`cnumpy.core.multiarray\n_reconstruct\np0`). `replay/c06/q0/gt_64k #630141` is 3.0M tokens of raw gzip bytes. `replay/c01/q4/gt_64k #25134` repeats `Amazon Transcribe` for 75k tokens. `replay/c04/q4/gt_64k #1` is a 1.77M-token survey CSV in the top quality tier.

### 3. Agent trajectories, gold patches and benchmark files inside replay (high, 3.6% of mix)

- 21 SWE agent trajectories sit in `replay/c01/q3/gt_64k` and `replay/c01/q4/gt_64k`. 17 are labelled failed. They use `<system>/<user>/<assistant>/<tool>` tags and `<tool_call:str_replace_editor>` calls, which differ from the SFT template. Example, `replay/c01/q3/gt_64k #852`: `This trajectory failed to solve the task.\n\n<system>\nYou are OpenHands agent`.
- 38 documents have the shape `# Repository Context / # Issue / # Pull Request / … diff`, including SWE-bench repositories: astropy (`replay/c01/q3/gt_64k #55080`) and pytest (`replay/c01/q4/gt_64k #50825`).
- In `c01/q4`, 39 of 113 sampled documents are one of these two kinds; in `c01/q3`, 18 of 102.
- `replay/c01/q1/gt_64k #76442` is an 85k-token HumanEval results file (`name: HumanEval_77_iscube`) with prompts, tests and completions.

### 4. Machine-translation damage in Nemotron multilingual v1 (high, 8.2% of mix)

The v1 subsets (`multilingual_v1/*`, translated with Qwen2.5-14B) carry the damage. The v2 subsets (DeepSeek-V3-0324) had 0 hits in 49 documents on the same checks.

| Flaw | Prevalence | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Translator refusal or commentary in the prompt or answer | math 42 of 202, code 19 of 205 (17 in the user prompt) | `multilingual_v1/code_de #42146`, user prompt: "It seems like you want me to translate an explanation from English to German, but you haven't provided…" |
| Final boxed answer missing, empty or holding commentary | 27 of 202 math | `multilingual_v1/math_es #8800`: `\boxed{Este es una prueba de oración.}` |
| Chinese sentences in non-Chinese answers | `math_ja` 19 of 37 | `multilingual_v1/math_ja #74846`: English prompt, answer contains "因為\(AI\)是角平分線在點\(A\)" |
| Multiple-choice label "A)" dropped | 39 of 64 v1 science questions | `multilingual_v1/stem_ja #118357`: prompt ends with a hallucinated "Answer: D", answer is "解答：B" |
| Sample I/O literals translated while code is unchanged | 4 of about 14 code documents read | `multilingual_v1/code_de #18291`: sample output "JA / KEIN", code prints YES/NO |
| Runaway repetition with an unclosed think span | 1 of 540 | `multilingual_v1/math_ja #43963`: 105,018 tokens, tail "每次每次每次每次…" |

Think spans are English in all 540 documents and are 78–91% of characters. No instruction tells the model which language to answer in.

### 5. Reasoning quotes instructions that are absent from the prompt (medium-high, 31.0% of mix)

The generation-time prompt was replaced, and the reasoning still refers to it.

- Python competitive coding: 194 of 280 think spans cite a `.buffer`/StringIO rule that the user turn does not contain. `competitive_coding_python #139390`: "Never use sys.stdin.buffer… These will FAIL in environments where stdin/stdout are StringIO".
- C++ competitive coding: 147 of 278 cite "C++17" where the prompt says "C++". `competitive_coding_cpp #2936`: "the instructions say: 'Please use C++17…'".
- `math_v3`: 213 of 973 think spans quote "Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}"; the user turn uses a different template. `math_v2/high`: 54 of 331 (`#157425`).
- `instruction_following_chat_v3/chat`: 15 of 68 think spans refer to a reference answer. `#205034`: "(This matches the provided good response)".

### 6. Agent traces claim success without evidence (high to medium, 15.4% of mix)

| Source | Prevalence | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `open_swe_traces/*` | All 650 end in a submit. Last visible test output shows failures in 51. About 13% explain failures as pre-existing or unrelated. | `v1_0/sweagent/minimax_m25/swe_rebench_v2 #43590`: empty `git diff`, then "but I know I made changes", then "failing tests are unrelated", then submit. `v1_1/openhands/qwen36_27b/swe_rebench_v2 #2053`: "Perfect! 4 out of 5 tests pass, and the 1 failure is a pre-existing issue". |
| `nemotron_sft_v3/swe_v1/r2e_gym`, `swe_v2/openhands_swe` | 93 of 93 end in a success claim, 90 with an emoji; 6 dismiss a failing test unverified | `swe_v1/r2e_gym #373`: "The one failing test is about HTTP/1.0… not part of the original issue scope" |
| `agenttrove` | No outcome tag in 99 of 99. 18 stop mid-task. 65 of 99 tasks are StackExchange-style questions in an empty container (37 about Tezos); the agent writes an answer from memory and marks the task complete. | `#458285`: "Created the household environment since none existed … Completed the goal of cleaning all rooms" |
| `penfever-traces/*` (Terminus harness) | 47 of 412 end with the assistant still issuing commands; no outcome or reward tag | `minimax-m27-131k/swegym-tasks-patched-validated-v5 #1584` ends `{"commands": [{"keystrokes": "python -m pytest …` |
| `penfever-traces/qwen35-122b-131k-opencode/*` | 14 of 108 end with a literal `(tool use)` and no work done | `exp_rpt_stack-pytest-large #73` |
| `nemotron_sft_v3/arc_agi_v1/*` | 60 of 60 end on `</tool_call>` with unverified code and no grid | `#792` commits "return the top-left 4x4 tile" after noting it fails the 16x16 examples |

### 7. One teacher reasons about hidden tests (high, 2.7% of mix)

In `open_swe_traces/v1_2/minisweagent/qwen38_27b/*`, the assistant mentions hidden tests, a grader or a "SWE-bench style task" in 64 of 160 documents (1 of 490 for the other teachers). No prompt mentions hidden tests. In 44 of 160 it recalls the upstream fix from memory.

- `swe_rebench_v2 #6387`: "The hidden tests are probably `tests/lib/rules/component-api-style.js` from that PR… Let me recall the actual implementation from v7.18.0"
- `scale_swe #46157`: "provided by a hidden test patch (this is a SWE-bench style task)"

### 8. Harness warnings that contradict the rendered turn (medium, 2.8% of mix)

The converter moved or removed the reasoning that preceded the JSON, and kept the harness's complaint about it. The model sees a clean JSON turn followed by a warning.

- `agenttrove`: 271 of 895 assistant turns (62 of 99 documents). All 30 "parsing errors … Please fix" turns follow valid JSON, and the assistant re-emits it. `#130952`: "WARNINGS: - Extra text detected before JSON object".
- `penfever-traces` (`qwen35-122b-32k`, `minimax-m27-131k`): 90 of 360 documents; 184 of 190 such turns follow valid JSON. `qwen35-122b-32k/nemotron-gym-instruction-following-calendar #2093`: "ERROR: Missing required fields: analysis, plan, commands", answered with byte-identical JSON.

### 9. Template inconsistencies (medium)

From the scripted audit of all 5,280 SFT documents:

| Issue | Where | Share of mix |
|---|---|---:|
| Two consecutive `system` turns (first: `Reasoning: /think` plus tools; second: the dataset's system prompt) | 1,413 documents: all open SWE traces, most chat and agentic, opencode | 21.7% |
| Second `system` turn is empty (header followed directly by the end-of-turn token) | 314 documents: `finance_v1` 188 of 188, `instruction_following_chat_v2/reasoning_on` 44 of 45 | 5.2% |
| Two tool protocols: `<tool_call>` JSON with `tool` turns (25.3%), and Terminus JSON in plain text with results in `user` turns (2.8%) | `agenttrove #10416` for the second | 28.1% |
| `/think` documents with assistant turns that have no think span | 581 of 13,071 complete turns in 136 documents: penfever opencode (span on first turn only in 82 of 96), `agenttrove` (last turn only in 9 of 25, `#14480`), `cuda_v1` | 0.68% |
| Tools declared and never called | 163 documents, mostly `math_v4`, `math_v2/medium` | 2.5% |
| User message wrapped in literal quotes | 223 opencode documents, e.g. `opencode_v1/agent_skills #4479` | 2.1% |

- Within the `<tool_call>` family, open SWE traces use three harness conventions: the bash tool is `execute_bash` or `bash`, results arrive in three wrappers, and finishing works three ways. Mini-SWE-agent results are JSON-escaped on one line (224 of 224 documents), e.g. `qwen38_27b/swe_rebench_v2 #2444`: `arg) && !arg.is_global_set())\n+ .collect::<Vec<_>>();`.
- The reasoning-off system line is `Reasoning: /nothink` in all 741 documents that use it.
- Reasoning effort has no signal. `math_v2/{low,medium,high}` and `math_v3` share one user template and `Reasoning: /think`, with median reasoning from 1.8k to 17k characters. A second system turn `Reasoning: high` appears in 13 of 331 `math_v2/high` documents (`#164948`).

### 10. Verbosity and teacher habits (medium)

- About 96% of competitive-programming tokens and about 99% of `openthoughts4-code-glm-5.2-n4` tokens sit inside one think span. 64 of 83 OpenThoughts4 documents exceed 32k tokens and 29 exceed 100k. `openthoughts4-code-glm-5.2-n4 #1293` (175k tokens) counts characters by hand: "r(1)a(2)n(3)d(4)o(5)m(6).(7) = 7".
- `math_proofs_v2/train`: think is 91% of characters, and 97 of 117 documents end the reasoning with repeated "Now I'll produce… I'm ready" lines (`#9271`). 86 of 117 are grading tasks, with verdicts skewed to full marks.
- `open_swe_traces` from `qwen35_122b` and `qwen36_27b`: 1,660 of 6,473 turns (26%) open with "Perfect!", "Excellent!", "Great!" or "Good!", against 50 of 3,907 for other teachers. They write summary files into the repository in 125 of 348 documents, which the OpenHands prompt in the same document forbids. `v1_1/sweagent/qwen36_27b/swe_rebench_v2 #3050`: `rm -f CHANGES_SUMMARY.md FINAL_CHECKLIST.md FIX_EXPLANATION.md README_FIX.md SOLUTION_SUMMARY.md VERIFICATION.md`.
- `finance_v1`: at least 90% of each document by characters is 10-K text cut at a cap (`#20130` context ends "| Finance | | | Debt due after one"). Answers were grounded and correct in the 15 checked. gpt-oss typography (U+202F) appears in 173 of 188 answers.
- Customer-service agents fabricate facts in 3 of about 8 read. `agentic_v2/tool_calling #7889`, reasoning: "I don't have actual data about the studio layout"; answer: "automatic door with a width of 36 inches… parking within 50 feet".

### 11. Harness-heavy and contrived agent data (medium)

- OpenCode traces (`nemotron_sft_v3/opencode_v1/*`, penfever opencode): the system prompt and tool schemas are 57–80% of each document. Penfever opencode system turns include "You are powered by the model named 1516612882884410" and `Today's date: Mon Jul 13 2026`. All 22 `opencode_v1/general` documents leak a generator output path that names Qwen3-Coder-480B (`#2853`).
- Penfever `nemotron-gym-*` sets (116 documents) answer a question by writing it to `/app/answer.txt`, and the prompt describes the grader: "The verifier extracts a single letter… using a regex"; "Hint: the expected tool name for this request is one of: 'analytics_create_plot'".
- Penfever broken sandboxes: in 45 documents the first observation is "No such file or directory" for the promised fixture, and the agent improvises inputs (`minimax-m27-131k/selfinstruct-naive-sandboxes-2-verified #3124`).
- Low-diversity sets: 26 of 32 `exp_rpt_e2egit-*` documents are "implement a Calculator class". `llm-verifier-freelancer` is raw scraped job postings.

### 12. Smaller findings

- **Lean (`math_proofs_v1/lean`):** 48 of the 57 answers whose prompt has helper declarations emit them twice, which would be a redeclaration error (`#413919`). 2 of 164 answers contain `sorry` (`#231906` is the six-`sorry` skeleton). No Lean compiler was run.
- **Ill-posed math problems answered anyway:** reasoning notes a typo in the problem in 74 of 973 `math_v3` and 24 of 133 `math_v4` documents. `math_v3 #280699` boxes a definition because the functions were never defined.
- **Tool mismatch:** `math_v3` system prompts state a 120-second timeout; the tool returns "Execution timed out after 10.0 seconds" in 54 turns.
- **Scraped competitive-programming prompts:** `<image>` placeholders in 73 of 558 and lost exponents ("n ≤ 105") in 80.
- **Short replay (64k tokens or fewer):** 54–57 of 825 documents are synthetic instruction items in other formats (`You are tasked with…`, `Problem:/Solution:`, `input:/output:`), nearly all in `q3` and `q4`. Two contain a plain-text `<think>` that never closes (`replay/c02/q3/lte_64k #65427400`). 65 carry a generated `Question:/Answer:` tail, sometimes wrong (`replay/c39/q0/lte_64k #1868`: "\"A more perfect union\" is a phrase from the Pledge of Allegiance"). By reading, 35–40% of this slice is LLM-rewritten web text.
- **Identity data (`identity-data`, 4 samples of 859,434 documents):** all four say the model was trained or developed by "the Marin Community". `#117405` does not deny "trained by OpenAI, right?". `#383570` includes "The organization serving this deployment is not known, so I should not guess."
- **Safety (8 samples):** 5 refuse. Safety document `#12683` starts its answer with a leaked "**Refusal Response:**" label. `#22471` refuses a fictional news story as "misinformation".
- **Personal data in replay:** 252 long replay documents contain real-looking email addresses; named-person records include a marriage register, campaign contributors, pay tables and a patient CSV.

### Checked and found clean

- All 5,280 SFT documents have one `<|begin_of_text|>` at offset 0 and end in `<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>`. Roles are `system`, `user`, `assistant`, `tool`. Every document starts with a system turn.
- Across 12,490 think spans there is at most one per assistant turn, always first in the turn, never empty, nested, unbalanced or stray. `/nothink` documents have zero spans in 9,586 turns. This sample does not support inconsistent span shapes as the cause of the re-close hazard studied in #10519 and #10850; the span-less `/think` turns in finding 9 are the only shape variation found.
- No foreign chat-template markers (`<|im_start|>`, `[INST]`, `<|python_tag|>`, `<|eom_id|>`) in SFT or replay, outside the replay trajectories in finding 3.
- No assistant names itself or a teacher's maker. No live-looking API keys or tokens.
- No identical documents. 15 groups (34 documents) share a first user message.
- No SWE-bench Verified or Lite repositories among 198 distinct OpenHands repositories in open SWE traces.
- No SFT document exceeds 262,144 tokens.

## Recommended changes

Ordered by expected benefit against cost. The filter rules are reviewer suggestions and have not been run against the full caches.

1. **Filter the long-context replay.** Drop documents with zlib ratio under about 0.12, a templated-line fraction over 0.6, base64 or binary content, or mean line length over 400. Cap length at 262,144 tokens. Drop documents that start `This trajectory ` or `# Repository Context`.
2. **Remove give-up endings and limit reasoning length.** Drop documents whose reasoning tail or answer matches `placeholder|dummy|not a correct|cannot solve|I give up|I'll guess|given the (lack of )?time`. Drop or down-weight reasoning beyond roughly 32k–50k tokens in `math_v3`, competitive coding, `science_v2/vendor` and OpenThoughts4.
3. **Drop or filter Nemotron multilingual v1.** Keep v2. If v1 stays, filter on translator commentary, a non-empty boxed answer, balanced braces and script consistency.
4. **Fix conversion artifacts.** Merge double system turns and drop empty ones. Strip harness warnings when the preceding rendered turn parses. Relabel `/think` documents with span-less turns as `/nothink` or drop them. Decode mini-SWE-agent tool results to plain text. Unquote opencode user turns and scrub the generator path. Restore the generation-time prompt where reasoning quotes it.
5. **Filter agent traces on outcome.** Join open SWE traces to resolve labels if they exist. Drop rollouts that end mid-task, end in `(tool use)`, or excuse failing tests. Keep AgentTrove tasks that have task files and a recorded pass. Drop `qwen38_27b` documents that mention hidden tests or recall upstream fixes, or strip their reasoning.
6. **Remove question answering from the terminal harness.** Drop or down-weight penfever `nemotron-gym-*` sets.
7. **Run instance-level decontamination** against HumanEval, SWE-bench, R2E-Gym, SWE-Gym, Terminal-Bench, Defects4J and KernelBench.
8. **Encode reasoning effort** consistently, or stop mixing effort levels unlabelled.
9. **Normalise teacher habits:** "Perfect!" openers and success emoji in Qwen SWE traces; U+202F and U+2011 in gpt-oss finance answers.
10. **Review `identity-data` separately** with a larger sample.

## Status

Review complete. No filters have been applied and no retraining has been run.

Limits:

- Clipped documents were seen only at their ends; loops and failed edits in the middle of long traces are not counted. About 6.5% of each long replay document was visible.
- No code was run, no Lean was compiled and no answer key was used. Wrong answers were counted only when the document admitted them.
- Regex counts are lower bounds, each spot-checked on about 10 hits.
- Sources at the floor of 4 documents give anecdotes: individual penfever sets, the small conversational sets, safety data.
- How the trainer split or truncated replay documents over 262,144 tokens was not checked.
- Whether user, system and tool turns carry loss was not checked. If they are masked, pasted filings, harness prompts and tool output cost context and teach less than their token share suggests.
- Benchmark overlap was matched by repository and dataset name. No instance-level join was run.
- Reviewer counts and excerpts were not independently re-derived.

## Links

* Review sample (30-day temporary prefix): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/sft-mix-viewer/review-2026.11.10-seed1/samples.parquet` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fsft-mix-viewer%2Freview-2026.11.10-seed1%2Fsamples.parquet))
* SFT Mix Viewer, a separate uniform sample (8 documents per SFT store, 4 per replay cache) with text, token and token-id views: https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/378c3d80-275c-49f2-9913-0bd2c292c354/
* Mix definition and sampler: `infra/marina/apps/sft_mix_viewer/` on branch `dml/sft-mix-viewer` (not yet pushed or merged)
* Model: https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05
* Related: #10400, #10519, #10850, #9212

## Decision Log

* 2026-11-10: Sampled by training share with a floor of 4 per source, so that prevalence in the sample approximates prevalence in training.
* 2026-11-10: Reviewed long documents as head plus tail. Mid-document rates are therefore lower bounds.

## Conclusion

The rendered template is consistent. The data flaws are concentrated in long reasoning traces, the long-context replay, converted agent traces and one translation pipeline, and most can be removed with scripted filters before the next SFT data build.

spillover_issues.title: [sft] Data review of the 10.05 SFT mix: flaws in a 7,503-document sample

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Snowball (10/05 SFT) often writes broken JSON for Pi's nested `edit` tool call, and the episode ends there. In an RL pass-rate screen (128 SWE-smith tasks × 8 tries, Pi 0.87.0), 575 of 1,024 tries ended on a malformed call. 524 of the 576 malformed spans were `edit` calls. The SFT data contains almost no calls in Pi's nested edit shape. Plan: add a slice of valid nested edits to SFT and measure the malformed-edit rate.

## Description

Pi's edit tool takes `{"path": …, "edits": [{"oldText": …, "newText": …}, …]}`, a list of objects inside the arguments object. The 10/05 SFT data has about 2.7M flat `str_replace_editor(command, path, old_str, new_str)` calls and essentially no Pi-shape edits.

Measured in the screen above:
- 1,093 edit calls; 523 failed `json.loads`.
- 362 of the 524 broken edit spans parse after one insertion at the JSON error offset: `]}` for 259, `}` for 103. This is a syntax-only check. It does not show that the repaired edit applies or fixes the task.
- 14 of the 575 broken-call tries still scored 1, so a malformed final call does not always mean a failed task.

Examples are viewable in the eval trace viewer (Marina login required): https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/943a733c-1d78-4b3b-8d7c-060aefb8726e/, run "Pass-rate 43604". Missing `]}`: attempts `010d96c8bd03428fb13da34e880a3a73` (step 18) and `0288247ea31c47e48cbb5c7ee3b6a467` (step 11). Missing `}`: `04741406ca5a4ff38401423e48ccd4ad` (step 18).

An A/B with a flat replacement edit tool (16 tasks × 2 arms × 4 tries) solved 20/64 vs 7/64 for Pi's native tool. Malformed calls not caused by the output cap were 3 vs 25. A larger confirmation (128 tasks × 8 per arm) is pending review. Third-party harnesses fix their own tool schemas, so a flat tool would only help our own harness.

The SFT training data's tool calls are well-formed: 452 of 47,399,691 assistant call spans failed a delimiter and `json.loads` check, across 51 scanned sources.

## Hypothesis or Goal

The model learned the flat edit shape in SFT and miscounts brackets in Pi's nested shape. Adding valid nested-edit calls to SFT should cut the malformed-edit rate without lowering other scores.

## Status

- E12-B data built: 1,000 train / 100 val / 100 test synthetic Pi edit exercises from TMax code (ODC-BY), 1–4 edits per call, 393,750 supervised tokens in train. Each edit was checked to restore the target file exactly. [Manifest](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Farm-b-20261114-r1%2Fmanifest-r1.json) (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/arm-b-20261114-r1/manifest-r1.json`).
- 1 h version: three 15-update arms (general-only control, E12 full, E12 attention/head only) trained and exported; Micro210 readout next.
- 8 h version: C150 recipe plus a grown E12-B set (~6k rows, at most 4 passes per row, about 0.8% of supervised tokens), against the existing C150 arm. It waits for the 1 h readout.
- Mochi: in its BFCL ×5 Pi traces, 1,445 tool calls parsed, and at most 3 messages left tool-call-like text unparsed. BFCL rarely uses `edit` (7 calls, none with more than one edit), so this does not test the nested-edit problem.

Readout: malformed-edit rate on Micro210's Pi trials, the Micro210 score paired by task, and the retention panel. Carry the slice into the next SFT stage if the malformed-edit rate falls by at least half against the matched control with no Micro210 or retention loss.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

- 2026-11-16: Do not train on the screen's own successful calls; those tasks are the readout panels.
- 2026-11-16: Keep Pi's native edit tool for reported benchmarks.

## Conclusion

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Protocol FAIL; original preregistered confirmation claim FALSE.** The run completed, but the strict tool-contract check failed. The numbers below are descriptive, not a confirmed flat-edit effect or a promotion decision.

We compared Pi’s native nested edit arguments with a flat replacement on the same 128 SWE-smith training tasks, eight attempts per arm: 2,048 assignments. There were 2,024 verified binary outcomes and 24 masked/unknown outcomes, which were not counted as failures.

| Descriptive reading | Control wins / known | Flat wins / known | Complete task profiles | Flat-minus-control task-profile difference | Conditional 95% interval |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| As recorded | 161 / 1,011 | 307 / 1,013 | 120 | **+14.38 percentage points** | +10.21 to +18.85 |
| Two affected attempts excluded | 161 / 1,011 | 305 / 1,011 | 118 | **+14.30 percentage points** | +9.96 to +18.75 |

The second reading removes two verified flat-arm wins from the pooled sensitivity only: nominal denominators become 1,024 control and 1,022 flat. The 13 control and 11 flat unknowns remain unknown. For the separate balanced eight-per-arm task comparison, the two affected task profiles become incomplete and are omitted; their other 30 outcomes remain pooled. The original endpoint is unchanged. These intervals condition on the observed complete task profiles; they do not cover excluded-task uncertainty, shared-run dependence, training-repeat variation or population generalization.

**Why strict confirmation failed:** two flat-arm attempts contained 65 requests using the native nested edit schema. Contracts were checked in 1,015 attempts per arm: zero affected control attempts and two affected flat attempts. Unchecked attempts and incomplete guard exposure are not assumed clean.

**Supported explanation:** in both cases, the outer agent ran `pi submit` through its bash tool. Pi 0.87 treats `submit` as a prompt, not a submission command. The resulting recorded requests use the default native tools; the outer flat extension was supplied through explicit CLI flags that the child commands omitted. The parent’s flat requests resume afterward with its prior context preserved. Pinned source and retained command/request/tool-result ordering support a recursive CLI invocation explanation, rather than an established parent compaction switch. Captured OS ancestry, every child setting/binary, original HTTP traffic and the effect of those calls on reward were not proved. This explanation does not repair the protocol failure.

Independent review reproduced the archive/grid joins, counts, bootstrap intervals and both sensitivities. Cost was **26.20 requested H100-hours**, not a utilization or invoice measurement. Native jobs and containers completed; exact GPU Pod absence/provider release has not yet been established. No new run, harness change or training-data promotion follows from this result.
